pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Savanna & Grassland Animals (ages 7–9): open, grassy habitats with few trees where survival turns on being seen from far off — driving herding, speed, and predator-prey dynamics.
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1 'Living things and their habitats' and Y4 adaptation; introduces the idea that a habitat's OPENNESS shapes behaviour (herds, watchfulness) not just body features.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 (diversity across habitats); 3-LS4-3 (survive well/less well in a habitat) — and seeds the predator-prey survival relationship developed later.
• Operational details: anchor on the African savanna cast (zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe as prey/grazers; lion, cheetah, hyena as predators) and the key ideas — safety in numbers (herds/dazzle), speed and endurance, many eyes watching, and grazing that tracks seasonal grass and water (migration). Establish that open grassland gives little cover, so both hunters and hunted rely on speed, distance, and group behaviour.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name savanna grazers and predators and say who eats whom. B (transitional, ~8–9): explain one way a herd helps prey survive (many eyes, confusion, dilution). C (formal, ~9): explain how open habitat drives both speed AND grouping, and link grazing movement to seasonal grass/water.
bestPractices: Root the habitat's demands in its openness — no trees to hide behind — so pupils derive herding, watchfulness and speed rather than memorising them.
Introduce 'safety in numbers' with concrete mechanisms (more eyes to spot danger; confusion of a moving mass; each individual less likely to be the one caught) instead of a slogan.
Frame predator vs prey as a fair two-sided problem (the cheetah must be fast AND close; the gazelle must be fast AND alert) to prepare the later arms-race idea without over-claiming.
Link grazing herds to seasonal grass and water so pupils see behaviour responding to a changing habitat, connecting to migration.
keyRepresentations: An open savanna scene with a grazing herd and a stalking predator at a distance — emphasising sightlines across open ground.
A 'many eyes' diagram showing a herd's overlapping fields of view vs a lone animal's blind spots.
A predator-prey chase pairing speed/stamina bars for cheetah vs gazelle.
A seasonal map showing herds moving to follow green grass and water.
commonMisconceptions: 'Predators always catch their prey' — most hunts fail; prey defences and group living work often.
'Being in a big group makes you an easier target' — herding usually lowers each individual's risk (dilution, confusion, shared vigilance).
'Savanna is a jungle/forest' — it is open grassland with scattered trees, and that openness is the point.
'The fastest animal always wins' — endurance, alertness, timing and cover matter as much as top speed.
'Grazers wander randomly' — herd movements track seasonal grass and water.

learn.summary: Savanna and grassland animals (ages 7–9): help pupils see that OPEN grassland with few trees for cover — where animals are visible from far off — favours herding, watchfulness and speed, while seasonal rains that change where grass and water are found drive seasonal movement. The anchor cast is African savanna herbivores/plant-eaters (zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe) and predators (lion, cheetah, hyena), with American grassland parallels (bison, prairie dogs). The central, hard-to-fake idea is that grouping changes survival ODDS: in a big, alert herd many eyes spot danger early, the moving mass confuses a hunter, and each individual is less likely to be the one caught (dilution). The preferred approach lets children operate this as a probability system; alternatives (sortable scene, matching/categorisation checks, outdoor tag game, guide-in-role hook) target naming, assessment, and curiosity. Address the misconceptions that predators always win, that a big group is an easier target, that savanna is a jungle, that the fastest always wins, and that plant-eaters wander randomly.

activities.title: Run the hunt: a safety-in-numbers simulation
feedback: When a learner leaves one gazelle alone and it is caught, prompt: what could a herd have done that this lone animal could not? (spot the predator sooner; make it hard to single out one target).
If a learner expects the big group to be caught more easily, point to the survival-rate meter across several runs and ask them to compare lone vs herd outcomes.
When they buff the predator and survival drops, ask what the prey could change (larger herd, higher vigilance) to show the problem is two-sided.
After the season toggle, ask why the herd had to move, linking grazing to following green grass and water.
activities.rationale: Survival odds are a dynamic, probabilistic system; letting children vary herd size and vigilance and observe changing catch rates over repeated runs is intended to make 'many eyes', confusion and dilution concrete rather than a memorised phrase. Optional interaction details (sliders, a survival-rate meter, a season toggle) are illustrative examples of the mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms, and the displayed survival numbers are illustrative rather than measured real-world probabilities.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
Savanna is open grassland with scattered trees; large grazers migrate seasonally to follow grass growth and water (e.g. Serengeti wildebeest).
Open-habitat behaviour (herding, vigilance) extends KS1/KS2 habitat-and-adaptation content to behavioural adaptation.
learnerActions: Set a prey herd's size (from a lone animal up to a large herd) and how alert/watchful the animals are, then release a predator (lion or cheetah) and watch the chase play out.

Run repeated hunts and read a survival-rate meter that updates across runs, comparing a lone dozing gazelle (caught almost every time) with the same gazelle in a big, watchful herd (spotted early, the mass scatters, most hunts fail).
Make the hunt two-sided: increase the predator's speed or stamina and discover the prey must group tighter and stay more alert to keep surviving.
Use a season toggle that moves grass and water so the herd must relocate to keep feeding, connecting behaviour to seasonal migration.
activities.intendedInsight: Safety in numbers is not a slogan but a reduction in each individual's risk — from more eyes watching, confusion of a moving mass, and dilution — and open habitat with little cover is WHY large hoofed prey such as zebras and gazelles rely mainly on grouping, alertness and speed rather than hiding (burrowers like prairie dogs can still hide underground).

activities.title: Outdoor tag: does a crowd protect the target?
feedback: If a learner predicted the crowd would make the target easier to catch, compare the two timed runs and ask what the milling crowd did to the lion's chase.
If a learner says the zebras win by ganging up on the lion, note that in the game nobody tags the lion back — any protection came from being hard to single out, not from fighting.
Ask the probe questions to deepen: what must the herd do first, before any running? Would one zebra alone be safer or in more danger? Is the lion 'bad' for hunting, and why does it hunt?
Ask the open-habitat contrast: if there were thick trees everywhere instead of open grass, would a big herd still help in the same way?
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–compare body activity is offered to surface and test the 'a crowd is easy to catch in' misconception using children's own movement, making the confusion effect (difficulty singling out one target) observable. Because the lion must chase one named child, the game does not test dilution (the chance that someone else is the one caught); that idea is explored in the simulation. This is one concrete classroom enactment, not the only route to the idea.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Play a tag game outside. Name one child the 'target zebra'; a 'lion' must tag only that named child.
Before running, predict whether the lion catches the named zebra faster when the whole herd stays clumped and milling around that child, or when that child stands alone.
Run both versions and compare how quickly the lion catches the target each time.
Discuss what the clumped, moving crowd did and, if it was harder for the lion to catch the target, why it was harder to pick out and chase one child.
activities.intendedInsight: Running both versions is intended to let children observe whether a moving, clumped crowd protects the named target, challenging the naive guess that a crowd is easy to be caught in; where the crowd does protect the target, it is because a single individual becomes hard to single out.

activities.title: Explain how the herd helps
feedback: If a learner explains the herd only by friendship or family, reframe around the hunting lion: what does the group do the moment danger appears? Introduce 'more eyes' and 'harder to catch just one'.
If a learner says the herd stays together to gang up and fight the lion off, note that most prey flee rather than fight, and emphasise early warning and being hard to single out over combat.
If a learner calls the lion cruel or evil, establish that predators hunt to eat and survive — predator and prey is a natural relationship, not good-versus-bad.
If a learner only says 'safety in numbers' as a slogan, press for what the numbers actually do: early warning, and being harder to single out.
activities.rationale: Naming what the numbers actually do against a predator is hard to fake, so a social answer ('friends/family') and a mechanistic answer diverge clearly, discriminating genuine understanding from a memorised phrase. Requiring the learner to construct the explanation elicits produced reasoning rather than recognition; recognition alone would not elicit this produced explanation.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Read or listen to the scene: on the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone, and a lion is hunting nearby.
Write or say how being in a big group helps a single zebra stay safe — stating what the numbers actually DO against the predator.
Say whether the lion is a bad animal for hunting, and explain why the lion hunts at all.
Explain what it is about open grassland, rather than forest, that makes seeing danger early possible.
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation names a mechanism — many eyes spot the predator early, or the moving crowd makes any one animal hard to single out — and treats predator–prey as feeding and survival, not malice; it links open ground to spotting danger from a distance.

activities.title: Name the cast and match who eats whom
feedback: If a learner sorts a predator as a plant-eater, ask what that animal eats and whether it hunts other animals.
If questions reveal the belief that predators always catch their prey, point out that most hunts fail and prey defences often work.
If a learner thinks a big group is an easier target, revisit the simulation or tag outcomes showing lower individual risk in a herd.
Confirm the habitat idea: savanna is open grassland with scattered trees, not a jungle or forest.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and short questions assess the naming and relationship ideas and can surface the 'predators always win' and 'big group = easier target' errors; these check and consolidate knowledge but test rather than build the probabilistic intuition, so they work best alongside the simulation or body activity.
sourceClaims: Diversity of life across habitats and differential survival within a habitat; seeds predator-prey relationships.
Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Name at least five grassland/savanna animals (e.g. zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe, lion, cheetah, hyena; bison and prairie dogs in American grasslands).
Sort the animals into plant-eaters and hunters/predators, noting that adult elephants and adult giraffes are rarely hunted, though their young can be.
Match each predator to prey it hunts (e.g. lion → zebra) to build a simple food chain.
Answer short questions on why herds help prey and on whether most hunts succeed or fail.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can name the savanna cast, tell apart plant-eaters and predators, describe who eats whom, and begin to flag that most hunts fail and that a big group is not an easier target.

activities.title: Open-ground scene and optional safari-guide hook
feedback: Prompt comparison between the herd's overlapping fields of view and the lone animal's blind spots: who spots the predator first, and why?
If a learner thinks plant-eaters wander randomly, use the seasonal map to show herds following grass growth and water.
If the guide's story raises a claim (e.g. 'the fastest always wins'), redirect to a run of the simulation to check whether endurance, alertness and timing also matter.

Reinforce that the open setting, with few trees or bushes for cover, is the point — it is why large hoofed animals like zebras and gazelles cannot rely on hiding (though burrowers like prairie dogs can dive underground).
activities.rationale: A tappable scene and a guide-in-role add context, emphasise sightlines across open ground, and motivate the topic, but on their own they carry the behavioural payoff weakly; they are framed here as scaffolds feeding the operational and explanation activities rather than substitutes for them.
sourceClaims: Savanna is open grassland with scattered trees; large grazers migrate seasonally to follow grass growth and water (e.g. Serengeti wildebeest).
Open-habitat behaviour (herding, vigilance) extends KS1/KS2 habitat-and-adaptation content to behavioural adaptation.
learnerActions: Explore a savanna scene with a grazing herd and a stalking predator at a distance; tap predator and prey roles to reveal who eats whom.
Compare a 'many eyes' picture of a herd's overlapping fields of view with a lone animal's blind spots, and discuss what the herd can see that the lone animal cannot.
Look at a seasonal map showing herds moving to follow green grass and water, and say why the herds keep moving.
Optionally, hear a safari-guide-in-role describe the scene as a curiosity hook, then return to the simulation or explanation task to test the ideas raised.
activities.intendedInsight: Open sightlines across grassland with only scattered trees, overlapping herd vigilance, and seasonal movement are visible features that set up the deeper survival logic; the scene and guide spark interest but the probabilistic payoff is explored in the other activities.

constraints: Ground the habitat's demands in its OPENNESS — few trees or bushes to hide behind — so pupils derive herding, watchfulness and speed rather than memorising them.
Teach 'safety in numbers' with concrete mechanisms (more eyes to spot danger; confusion of a moving mass; each individual less likely to be the one caught) rather than as a slogan.

Frame predator vs prey as a fair two-sided problem (the cheetah must be fast AND close; the gazelle must be fast AND alert) to prepare the later arms-race idea without over-claiming evolutionary conclusions for this age band.

Address misconceptions explicitly: predators do NOT always catch prey (most hunts fail); a big group usually lowers individual risk rather than raising it; savanna is open grassland with scattered trees, not jungle; top speed alone does not decide outcomes (endurance, alertness, timing, cover matter); herbivore movement tracks seasonal grass and water, it is not random.

A tap-to-reveal scene and a guide-in-role chat are context and motivation scaffolds; on their own they do not let a child operate the survival-odds system, so pair them with the simulation or the body activity — this is a scoped limit, not a claim that such formats can teach nothing.

Matching/categorisation and short-answer questions assess and consolidate; by themselves they check classification rather than build the probabilistic intuition, and recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own constructed explanation.

The simulation's survival-rate meter should reflect that most hunts fail and that herding/vigilance lower each individual's risk; its numbers are illustrative, not measured real-world probabilities. Avoid implying predators nearly always catch prey or that larger groups are easier to catch.

Use accurate feeding labels: giraffes browse leaves and elephants are mixed feeders, so sort herbivores as 'plant-eaters' rather than calling the whole cast 'grazers'; note that adult elephants and adult giraffes are rarely hunted (their young are more at risk), so not every plant-eater is equally likely to be prey.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all four sources carry verified:false in the row, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Sources were not re-fetched; sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's claims and support the stated teaching principles only, not the empirical effectiveness of any specific activity.

The 'many eyes', confusion and dilution mechanisms and 'most hunts fail' come from an unverified behavioural-ecology reference; the simulation's numeric survival rates must be presented as illustrative, since no quantitative source is cited.
Keep the two-sided framing honest: the row seeds but does not establish a predator-prey 'arms race', so avoid over-claiming evolutionary conclusions with ages 7–9.

The legacy row framed the simulation as the only way the behavioural payoff can be 'felt' and dismissed 3D and quiz formats as merely testing; this has been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims about what a format can or cannot teach.

The original row labels giraffe and elephant as 'grazers'; giraffes browse leaves and elephants are mixed feeders. The sort was reframed as 'plant-eaters (prey) vs predators' and the summary updated so no learner-facing text hinges on the inaccurate 'grazer' label; the original simplification is recorded here only.

assess.poeTask: Play a tag game outside. Name one child the 'target zebra'; a 'lion' must tag only that child. Children predict whether the lion will catch the named zebra faster when the whole herd stays clumped and milling around that child, or when that child stands out alone. Run both and compare — the clumped, moving crowd protects the target, violating the naive 'a crowd is easy to catch in' guess.
probeDeeper: What is the very first thing the herd needs to do to stay safe — before any running?
Would one zebra alone be safer, or in more danger, than a zebra inside a herd? Why?
Is the lion a bad animal for hunting the zebra? Why does the lion hunt at all?
What if there were thick trees everywhere instead of open grass — would a big herd still help in the same way?
assess.correctAnswer: In a big herd there are many eyes and ears to spot the lion early and warn the others, and when they all run any one zebra is less likely to be the one caught — the moving crowd makes it hard for the lion to pick out and chase a single target. Safety comes from numbers, shared lookout and confusion, not from the zebras fighting the lion off.

errorPatterns.pattern: They stay in a herd because they're friends or it's their family, like people
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe around the hunting lion — ask what the group does the moment danger appears; introduce 'more eyes' and 'harder to catch just one'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because the zebras are all friends and like to be together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the herd by companionship with no link to the lion or to danger.

errorPatterns.pattern: The herd stays together so they can gang up and fight the lion off
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note that most prey flee rather than fight; emphasise early warning and being harder to single out over combat.
errorPatterns.distractor: So they can all attack the lion together and chase it away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes zebras attacking or scaring the lion as the main benefit of the group.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lions are bad or mean animals that kill for fun
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish predators hunt to eat and survive; predator and prey is a natural relationship, not good-versus-bad.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the lion cruel or evil; doesn't connect hunting to feeding and survival.

responseLevels.gap: Names savanna animals but explains herding only socially ('they're friends/family') with no link to predators.
responseLevels.full: Explains a mechanism — many eyes spot the predator early and any individual is less likely to be the one caught, or the moving crowd confuses the hunter — recognises predator–prey as feeding not malice, and links open grassland to being able to see danger coming.
responseLevels.partial: Connects the herd to the lion and says 'safety in numbers', but only as a slogan — can't say what the numbers actually do (early warning, harder to single out one), or thinks the benefit is ganging up to fight.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone. A lion is hunting nearby. How does being in a big group help a single zebra stay safe?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a social idea explains the herd by friendship or family and gives no survival mechanism. A child who understands names a mechanism — more eyes watching, or being harder to single out. Naming what the numbers actually DO against a predator is hard to fake, so the two answers diverge clearly.
